Patterns

A component is one brick: a card, a button, a row panel. A pattern is a fixed composition of bricks that already repeats on the screens: the frame of a pushed screen, the whole-screen message, a list of cards under its label. Each one below is built only from components on the components page, carries no CSS and no class of its own, and is copied from a real screen. The source of each is one file in design-system/patterns/.

A pattern exists only where it already stands on three screens. The build holds that rule: every screen a pattern names must exist in wireframes/ and still carry the classes the pattern is made of, and the names must add up to three screens once a screen's -empty, -error, -loading and service files are counted as that one screen. When a screen stops carrying a pattern, the build fails until the pattern or the screen is put right. A composition found on one or two screens stays in those screens and is not drawn here.

The desktop twins

The desktop twins in wireframes/desktop/ are screens too, and the same three-screen rule holds for them: a desktop pattern names twins (desktop/<name>), and their -empty, -error, -loading and service files are folded into their screen the same way. Five compositions stand on three or more twins: the Desktop step window (the pushed screen), the Desktop tab panel (the tab root), the Desktop message window, the Desktop waiting window and the Signed-out window. Each is the desktop reading of a phone pattern, built from the wide-screen components; none of them has CSS of its own. Their gaps were measured on the twins at 1600 × 900, and every departure from the proximity numbers or from HIG and WCAG is written into the pattern, not corrected in it.

Take the pattern when

  • The new screen does a job an existing screen already does. Arrived from elsewhere and ends in a decision: Pushed screen. One of the four tabs: Tab root. Nothing to show: Whole-screen message. Take the pattern's markup, keep its order, its zone labels and where its actions go, and change only the words and the data.
  • You would otherwise choose the order of parts yourself. The pattern has already settled it: outcome before record, label before panel, the primary above the secondaries, the exit inside the message or in the action bar but never both.

Build from components when

  • No pattern does the screen's job. Build it from the components, and if the same composition then reaches three screens it becomes a pattern here.
  • Only part of the screen changes. One zone failing is a Message block in that zone, not a whole-screen message; one fact is a note, not a panel.
  • The pattern almost fits. Do not bend a pattern with a modifier or an inline style. A pattern has no CSS to bend; a change of look is a change to a component, made in design-system/components/ and shown on every screen that uses it.

Looked for and not found

Three compositions were looked for and stand on fewer than three screens, so they are not patterns:

  • A list header with a filter. The finder with its filter drawer stands on listings only; the in-page tabs over a list stand on operator-listings and time-slot. Two screens.
  • The search home. It is one screen, and it is the Finder component.
  • The call. It stands on three screens but is one component, the Call surface.

Four desktop compositions were looked for and stand on fewer than three twins:

  • Hanging cards over the map. The orders or jobs as glass cards with no panel round them stand on order-history and operator-jobs. Two screens; the Hanging cards component carries them.
  • The side panel beside the route. It stands on tracking alone, its service and state files folded in. It is the Side panel component.
  • The outcome in a window with no head. It stands on delivery alone (with delivery-aerial); inspection-report has a head. It is Outcome in a window.
  • The wide window. call, chat, inspection-report and order-details-aerial carry .dr-window--wide, but measured at 1600 × 900 every one is 560 wide, like every other window (a later rule sets one width for all of them). They share a class, not a composition: the call and the chat are one component, the call and chat window, and the report and the details are step windows.

From desktop/job-brief.

  • .dr-desk with .dr-mapground and .dr-veil — the frame: the live map under everything, darkened at its edges.
  • .dr-whead — the header, unchanged from the tab the step was opened from: Overview · Activity · Help and the green Order for the client; Overview · Jobs · Earnings · Ratings for the operator.
  • .dr-deskrail--start and --end — the rails, unchanged from that tab.
  • .dr-dim — the map and the rails at 35% behind the window, so the step is what is read.
  • .dr-window — 560 wide (narrower on a narrow screen: below 1336 it keeps 64 of map to each rail, down to 420); below a 1600 window it starts on the rails' top line, 96, from 1600 up it is centred, min(640, the window − 232) tall, centred, one padding of 32 on all four sides.
  • .dr-window__head — the back, a round 48 icon button named Back to …, and the title. A step that cannot be left (the payment hand-over) has the title alone.
  • .dr-scroll — the content, the only part that scrolls, one group after another.
  • .dr-foot — the action, on the window's own glass; several actions stack, the primary on top.
  • .dr-talkdock — Talk to AI, waiting under the window.

Measured at 1600 × 900 on job-brief, order-setup, operator-signup and payment-error: the padding is 32 on every side; the head stands 32 above the content and the groups 24 apart (job-brief: the rows, then the notes card, 24); the action at least 24 under the content; back and title 12 apart in the head. Stacked actions stand 8 apart in .dr-window__actions and 12 in .dr-foot--stack. The head is a step further from the content than the groups are from each other, so it reads as the head; every gap inside a group is smaller than the 24 between groups, so the grouping holds.

Checked against the standards: the back is 48 × 48 (HIG · 44pt target, +4; WCAG 2.5.8 asks 24) and carries its name in aria-label alone (WCAG 4.1.2, microcopy.md D9); every button is 44 tall (HIG · 44pt, 0 to spare). Two departures, stated and not corrected:

  • Two green controls on a client step. The header's Order stays the green primary on every client screen (the designer's call, 2026-10-19), so a client step shows it beside the window's own primary. The operator's job-brief, which has no Order, has one. One green control per screen is the project's rule, not HIG's or WCAG's; neither standard is failed.
  • The window comes last in the reading order. In the markup the header and both rails come before main, so a keyboard user tabs through every rail card before reaching the step. WCAG 2.4.3 is met (the order is the same on every step), but WCAG 2.4.1 asks for a way to bypass repeated blocks and the twins have no skip link; the main landmark serves screen-reader users only.

From desktop/operator-signup.

The operator's sign-up comes before there is a day or a job to show: the same window with its head and foot, the header with the logo and the theme only, no rails and no Talk to AI. The gaps are the step's own: padding 32, the head 32 above the content, the two actions 8 apart.

Take the pattern

The screen is a step of a flow on the desktop, the phone's pushed screen: it is reached from a tab or from the step before, it ends in a decision, and it can be left by its back. Take the window, its head, its scroll and its foot; change only the words and the content of the scroll. When the actions must stay in view while a long body scrolls (contact-support, report-issue, account-edit), the window takes .dr-help-split; see Desktop window.

Build from components instead

  • The screen is one of the tabs: a Desktop tab panel, never a window over the dimmed map.
  • The whole content failed or is empty: a Desktop message window.
  • The screen is the wait itself, the route on the map: the side panel of tracking, not a window.
  • A call or a chat: the call and chat window, a component of its own.

Desktop tab panel

One of the tabs on the desktop: the phone's tab root drawn as one panel between the rails, in the window's place and size. The header shows which tab is open; there is no back and no dimmed map, because nothing was stepped into.

From desktop/wallet.

  • .dr-whead — the header; the open tab is the current link of .dr-whead__nav (aria-current="page"), Account is the profile chip.
  • .dr-deskrail--start and --end — the rails: the client's day and orders, or the operator's day, availability and jobs.
  • .dr-panel — 560 wide (narrower on a narrow screen: below 1336 it keeps 64 of map to each rail, down to 420); below a 1600 window it starts on the rails' top line, 96, from 1600 up it is centred, min(640, the window − 232) tall, centred between the rails, one padding of 32 on all four sides. No .dr-dim: the panel is the tab's own content.
  • .dr-panel__title — the tab's name as its h1. Where a display heading leads the content (account, support), the h1 stays for assistive tech only.
  • .dr-scroll — the content, one group after another; the zone labels are headings for screen readers and are drawn nowhere.
  • .dr-foot — the tab's one action (Withdraw, Edit profile, Contact support), the width of the panel.
  • .dr-talkdock — Talk to AI under the panel.

Measured at 1600 × 900 on wallet: the padding is 32 on every side; the title stands 32 above the content; the balance and the recent earnings are 24 apart; the action 24 under the content. Inside the list the earnings stand 8 apart (.dr-list--snug): the value the proximity rule gives the parts of one thing, not the 12 it gives the items of one list. A departure, recorded and not corrected: 8 is a third of the 24 between groups, so the list still reads as one group.

Checked against the standards: the open tab is named by aria-current and by a fill behind charcoal, not by colour alone (WCAG 1.4.1); every button is 44 tall (HIG · 44pt); a tab has no back (HIG · Tab bars: a tab is switched to, not pushed).

Desktop message window

The screen's content is missing or failed, so the window holds one message and its way out, and everything round the window stays as it was. It is the phone's whole-screen message on the desktop.

From desktop/payment-error.

  • The frame, the head and the rails — unchanged from the screen's base file, so the user is still where they were.
  • .dr-scroll holding one .dr-msg — what happened and what to do, in the middle of the space between the head and the foot. An error takes the red mark and role="alert", an empty state the neutral mark and role="status".
  • .dr-foot — the way out, always here and never inside the message (the designer, 2026-10-19: «CTA в нижньому барі картки»): Try again on top, the alternative under it.

Measured at 1600 × 900 on payment-error: the padding 32, the head 32 above the content, the message centred in what is left; inside the message the mark, the title and the body 12 apart; the two exits 8 apart. The message's 12 is the Message block's own rhythm, above the 4–8 the proximity rule gives the parts of one thing. A departure, recorded: it is half of the 24 that would split the message, so it still reads as one.

Checked against the standards: the message is announced without moving focus (WCAG 4.1.3: alert for an error, status for an empty state); no window is a dead end, every one has its exit in the foot (requires: dr-foot); the exits are 44 tall (HIG · 44pt).

From desktop/notifications-empty.

A tab with nothing to show keeps its panel and its title; the message takes the middle of the panel and the one way out stands in the foot. Measured on notifications-empty: the title 32 above the content, the message centred, the action at the foot.

Take the pattern

The whole content has nothing to show: an empty list, a failed load, a declined payment. A signed-out window takes it the same way, with no head (signin-error, onboarding-client-empty).

Build from components instead

Part of the content still holds. wallet-empty keeps the balance at the top and puts the message under it; operator-dispute-error keeps the job card; order-setup-empty keeps the form; tracking-error puts the message on the map beside the side panel. There the Message block is one group among the others.

Desktop waiting window

A hand-off the user waits on (Diia, the bank, Apple Pay, the search for an operator), drawn as the step's own window with one spinning mark in its middle. It is the phone's waiting outcome on the desktop.

Built from: Desktop window · Outcome · Skeleton · Button

Stands on 5 screens: desktop/operator-signup-loading, desktop/order-confirmed-loading, desktop/payment-loading, desktop/signin-loading, desktop/withdraw-loading

Composition

Sign in

Verifying your identity…

Confirming your details with Diia. This takes a few seconds.

Continue Cancel

From desktop/operator-signup-loading.

  • .dr-window with its head — the same window as the step before, so the wait reads as part of that step.
  • .dr-center — the milestone mark with the spinning glyph (.dr-spin), what is happening as the display line, and how long it takes as the lead; in the middle of the space between the head and the foot.
  • The skeleton lines the phone puts under the spinner stay in the markup and are drawn nowhere on the desktop: one indicator for one wait (HIG · Progress indicators).
  • .dr-foot — what the user can still do: Continue when the hand-off returns, Cancel under it. withdraw-loading has no foot: the transfer hands over on its own.

Measured at 1600 × 900 on payment-loading: the padding 32, the head 32 above the content, the mark, the display line and the lead 12 apart. The 12 is the outcome's own rhythm, above the 4–8 the proximity rule gives the parts of one thing. A departure, recorded: it is half of the 24 that would split the block, so it still reads as one.

Checked against the standards: the wait is announced (role="status" on the block or on its lead, WCAG 4.1.3); the glyph stops under reduced motion (reduced-motion.css; WCAG 2.3.3, HIG · Reduce motion) and the words still say what is happening.

Take the pattern

The screen waits on a hand-off whose progress it cannot show, and says what it is waiting for and for how long.

Build from components instead

The wait has a shape to show: a list or a form about to load is a Skeleton in its own place (order-review-loading, notifications-loading), not a spinner in the middle.

Signed-out window

Before sign-in there is nothing of the user's to show, so the desktop is the map, the logo, the theme and one window: what DRON is, then how to get in.

Built from: Desktop shell · Entry window · Onboarding slider · Pager · Identity mark · Button

Stands on 4 screens: desktop/onboarding-client, desktop/onboarding-operator, desktop/signin, desktop/welcome

Composition

Sign in to DRON

One verification lets you order drone services — or take jobs as a certified operator.

Diia and BankID confirm who you are. DRON never sees your password.

Continue with Diia Continue with BankID

By continuing you agree to the Terms & Privacy Policy.

From desktop/signin.

  • .dr-whead — the logo and the theme switch; no navigation, no Order, no profile chip.
  • No rails and no Talk to AI.
  • .dr-window.dr-entry — the centred window, 560 (narrower on a narrow screen: below 1336 it keeps 64 of map to each rail, down to 420); below a 1600 window it starts on the rails' top line, 96, from 1600 up it is centred × min(640, the window − 232), padding 32, with no head: the copy is held in the middle of the window (.dr-entry--flush sets it flush left).
  • .dr-entry__acts in .dr-foot — the ways in, stacked, the primary on top, the terms note under them.

Measured at 1600 × 900 on signin: the padding 32; the title, the lead and the note 8 apart; the two ways in 10 apart and the terms note 10 under them. The 10 sits between the 8 of the parts of one thing and the 12 of one group, so the actions and their note read as one group, far from the copy above them.

Checked against the standards: the buttons are 44 tall (HIG · 44pt); the window has no visible head and is named by aria-label (WCAG 4.1.2); the Diia and BankID marks are decorative (alt="") beside the words that name them (WCAG 1.1.1).

With the slider

Stands on: desktop/onboarding-client, desktop/onboarding-operator, desktop/welcome

You order, a pro handles it

Pick a service and pay. A certified DRON operator does the flying — you never touch the drone.

A verified, insured operator

The moment you pay you see their name, photo and live position. Someone accountable is on the way.

What the drone does — and doesn't

It flies a set route, keeps its distance, and only records what your order needs. Brief low noise on take-off and landing; no filming of your neighbours.

Get started Skip

From desktop/welcome.

The onboarding: one slide at a time, Previous and Next beside the picture, the pager under it, the actions at the foot. A mouse has no swipe, so the round 48 buttons are the single-pointer way through (WCAG 2.5.1), named (WCAG 4.1.2); on the first slide Previous is aria-disabled. A proximity departure, recorded and not corrected: measured on welcome, the pager stands 36 under the slider it belongs to and 16 above the first action, so by space alone it reads with the actions rather than with the slides it counts.

Take the pattern

The user is not signed in: the onboarding, the welcome, sign in. Take the bare header, the one window and the stacked ways in; change only the words and the slides.

Build from components instead

  • Role select is the same window with no foot: its two choices are the actions. It stands on one screen, so it is built from the Entry window and choice cards.
  • Switch role is reached signed in: the rails and Talk to AI stay round it.
  • The operator's sign-up has a back and a title: a Desktop step window before the rails.
